headline: High: shared filesystem and write-capable pair creates prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict risks; Copilot Workspace edits can cascade into unsafe actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b reads and writes editor buffers and repo context. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where agent_a-produced text can reach agent_b as trusted file or buffer content. The pair is not documented with direct interaction evidence, so uncertainty is handled conservatively.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into a file or MCP-fed buffer that agent_b later opens, injection is possible.
IF agent_b treats repo context or open buffers as authoritative instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer actions.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
Disable MCP routes that ingest untrusted text for agent_a.
Require human review of any agent_b edits before apply.
Prefix all inter-agent files with a non-executable data format.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures, while agent_b reads repo context and open editor buffers and can write files. If they share a workspace, sensitive material from agent_a can flow into agent_b outputs or vendor APIs. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository checkout, agent_b can read agent_a-produced artifacts.
IF agent_a places signatures or prompts into files, agent_b may transmit them through its vendor-backed context path.
mitigations: Use separate clones or directories.
Exclude secrets from shared files.
Turn off automatic context sharing in the editor.
Review outbound prompts for secret material before sending.
requires-engineering: enforce file-level access controls between agents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can modify git state and run subprocesses; agent_b can also modify git state and write files. Both support multiple instances, so concurrent edits to the same repo can race even though agent_b has no shell. The overlap is real but not enough evidence for the high-severity same-dir unrestricted-write case.
conditions: IF both agents commit or rewrite the same branch without locking, git conflicts can occur.
IF both write to the same files in one checkout, last-writer-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch.
Serialize commits with a lock file.
Use read-only mode for one agent during the other's write phase.
Run a quick diff before merge.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency locks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate outputs via MCP and shell-driven workflows, and agent_b's Workspace/chat model can apply edits from context. That makes it plausible for agent_b to treat agent_a output as authoritative unless a human verifies it. Direct evidence of this exact pair is absent, so the safer medium level fits.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-produced summaries without verification, incorrect facts can propagate into edits.
IF agent_a emits malformed commands or code snippets, agent_b may apply them as workspace changes.
mitigations: Require source links for any factual claim.
Have a human approve agent_b edits.
Compare agent_a output against the repo before acting.
Limit agent_a to draft-only outputs.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts and repository metadata, while agent_b handles source code and open editor buffers. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, and both profiles are closed-source/open-source mixed without a specific regulated-data flow. The only concrete issue is a general policy gap, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into shared repo context, policy review is needed.
IF retention settings differ between the editor and the MCP-backed agent, logs may diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared repos.
Check vendor retention settings.
Document which agent may see which data class.
Use a DPA where required.
requires-engineering: implement data-class routing controls.
